think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 5-year-old girl with Down syndrome from an endemic Amazonian rainforest valley presented with extensive, highly disfiguring, chronic disseminated ulcerative skin lesions spanning up to 8 cm and oral mucosal erosions with stridor, showing complete refractoriness to conventional antimonial and deoxycholate therapies. The clinical picture mimics deep endemic fungal granulomas (e.g., paracoccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis) and histiocytic malignancies (Langerhans cell histiocytosis), complicated by profound T-helper and B-cell immunodeficiency secondary to trisomy 21.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs upon transfer and admission to the tertiary pediatric hospital following clinical triage, complete physical examination of the disseminated mucocutaneous ulcers, pulmonary assessment, and baseline leukocyte and flow-cytometric immunophenotyping, immediately prior to skin punch biopsy histopathology, direct microscopic smear examination, Montenegro intradermal skin testing, serologic titers, and species-specific PCR-RFLP analysis.
3. Differential Distinctions: Deep cutaneous fungal granulomas were considered given the chronic destructive ulcerated plaques with mucosal erosions in an Amazonian resident, but periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining was negative. Langerhans cell histiocytosis and lymphoproliferative disorders were considered given the refractory pediatric presentation and Down syndrome, but CD1a immunohistochemistry was negative. Disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania (Viannia) braziliensis was confirmed by amastigotes on smear and biopsy, positive Montenegro reaction, positive indirect immunofluorescence, and PCR-RFLP, with complete cure achieved via liposomal amphotericin B.
case_prompt:
A 5-year-old female patient with a history of Down syndrome, residing in the province of Quillabamba within the department of Cusco, Peru—an Amazon jungle region—was referred and admitted to a tertiary pediatric institute due to progressive enlargement and widespread dissemination of cutaneous ulcerations. Her father reported that at the age of one year, the child initially developed papular lesions on the face that gradually increased in size and subsequently ulcerated over the right malar and mandibular regions. Over the ensuing four years, despite multiple empiric and targeted antimicrobial therapies (including courses of intravenous pentavalent antimonials, amphotericin B deoxycholate, oral miltefosine, and topical imiquimod) as well as an interim 3-month course of oral prednisone, the lesions proved refractory, continuously expanded, and disseminated to distant anatomical sites, with intermittent laryngeal stridor and dysphonia.

On physical examination upon admission, the patient had phenotypic features of Down syndrome. Dermatologic examination revealed multiple extensive ulcerations with infiltrated, raised, and rolled borders. The lesions were widely distributed across the face (chin), bilateral upper extremities (elbows and arms), bilateral lower extremities (legs), and buttocks, with individual ulcer diameters ranging from 1 cm on the limbs to 8 cm on the buttocks. Examination of the oral cavity demonstrated mucosal erosions measuring 0.5 cm. Respiratory examination revealed subcostal retractions and diffuse rhonchi across bilateral lung fields. The remainder of the systemic physical examination was unremarkable.

Initial triage laboratory evaluation demonstrated a total leukocyte count of 4,600 cells/mcL. Baseline flow-cytometric lymphocyte subset immunophenotyping revealed profound cellular immune alterations, characterized by severe T-helper and B-lymphocyte penia: CD3/CD4 lymphocytes of 258 cells/mcL (reference range: 500–2,700 cells/mcL), CD4 T-helper lymphocytes of 251 cells/mcL (reference range: 1,500–5,000 cells/mcL), regulatory T lymphocytes of 14 cells/mcL (reference range: 35–140 cells/mcL), CD8 cytotoxic T cells of 627 cells/mcL (reference range: 500–1,600 cells/mcL), B lymphocytes of 50 cells/mcL (reference range: 600–3,000 cells/mcL), and natural killer lymphocytes of 195 cells/mcL (reference range: 100–1,300 cells/mcL).

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: In a resident of the Amazon river basin with chronic ulcerative mucocutaneous granulomas and mucosal erosion, deep fungal infections were major considerations; ruled out by negative periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) fungal staining and absence of fungal structures on direct microscopy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Amastigote forms were found during direct microscopic examination (smear test); this procedure was carried out at the National Referral Laboratory of Leishmaniasis of the National Institute of Health since the periodic acid-Schiff stain (PAS) and the differentiation group 1A (CD1A) were negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Extensive destructive cutaneous ulcers refractory to medical therapies in a young child with Down syndrome raised suspicion for Langerhans cell histiocytosis or a lymphoproliferative disorder; ruled out by negative CD1a immunohistochemical staining.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Amastigote forms were found during direct microscopic examination (smear test); this procedure was carried out at the National Referral Laboratory of Leishmaniasis of the National Institute of Health since the periodic acid-Schiff stain (PAS) and the differentiation group 1A (CD1A) were negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Primary Immunodeficiency with Unresponsive Cutaneous Infection
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Refractory mucosal involvement and disseminated spread occurred in the context of Down syndrome-associated cellular immunodeficiency, verified by profound CD4 T-helper and B-cell lymphopenia on flow cytometry.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Laboratory tests showed the following: total leukocytes: 4600 cells/microL, CD3/CD4 lymphocytes: 258 cells/microL (normal range: 500-2700), regulatory T lymphocytes: 14 cells/microL (normal range: 35-140), T Helper CD4 lymphocytes: 251 cells/microL (normal range: 1500-5000 cells/microL), CD8 Cytotoxic T cells: 627 cells/microL (normal range: 500-1600 cells/microL), B lymphocytes: 50 cells/microL (normal range: 600-3000 cells/microL), and Natural Killer (NK) lymphocytes: 195 cells/microL (normal range: 100-1300 cells/microL).

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Skin punch biopsy revealed dense lymphohistiocytic dermal infiltration with abundant intracellular amastigotes, confirmed by direct microscopic smear examination, a positive Montenegro intradermal test (7 x 8 mm induration), an indirect immunofluorescence IgG titer of 1/160, and PCR-RFLP identifying Leishmania (Viannia) braziliensis. Due to resistance to conventional deoxycholate formulations and antimonials, high-dose intravenous liposomal amphotericin B was initiated, leading to complete ulcer healing.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Skin biopsy revealed hyperkeratosis, irregular epidermal hyperplasia, fibrous dermis with predominantly dense, lymphohistiocytic, inflammatory infiltrate with some plasma cells, and histiocytes with abundant structures suggestive of Leishmania spp. amastigotes. Amastigote forms were found during direct microscopic examination (smear test)... The Montenegro intradermal reaction test (IDRM) was positive, with a 7 x 8 mm induration at 48 hrs. Anti-Leishmania IgG antibodies were detected in the patients' serum by indirect immunofluorescence, with a positive titer of 1/160. Genomic DNA samples extracted from lesion tissue revealed that the disease was caused by Leishmania (Viannia) braziliensis... The patient was diagnosed with DL and treatment started with liposomal amphotericin B, 3 mg/kg/day intravenously every 5 to 6 days, she received 15 doses. Dermal infections were also treated. Patients' condition improved after the 11th dose (Figures 1B and 2B), up until the 15th dose (Figure 2C).
